title: AI-Powered Criminal Network Analysis System
department: National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB), Women Safety Division
description:
• Background Modern criminal activities are increasingly organized and interconnected. Criminals often operate through networks involving associates, intermediaries, financial channels, communication links,locations, and events. Law enforcement agencies collect large volumes of data from sources such as:
• FIRs and police reports
• Call Detail Records (CDRs)
• Financial transaction records
• Surveillance reports
• Social media intelligence
• Criminal history databases
• Intelligence agency reports Despite having access to this information, investigators frequently face challenges in identifying hidden relationships among suspects because the data is fragmented, unstructured, and distributed across multiple systems. Manual analysis can be slow, labor-intensive, and prone to missing critical connections.With advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML),Natural Language Processing (NLP), and Graph Analytics, it is now possible to automatically discover relationships, detect patterns, and generate insights that can assist investigators in understanding criminal networks more effectively.
• Description The objective is to develop an AI-powered system that can analyze large volumes of criminal and intelligence-related data to uncover hidden networks and relationships among individuals, organizations, locations,and events.
The system should:
• Collect and process data from multiple sources.
• Extract important entities such as people, locations, vehicles, phone numbers, and organizations.
• Build relationship maps showing how different entities are connected.
• Identify key individuals who play influential roles within criminal networks.
• Detect suspicious patterns and unusual activities.
• Assist investigators by providing visual and analytical insights.
• Expected Solution Develop an AI-powered system that automatically analyzes structured and unstructured crime-related data to uncover criminal networks,identify key influencers, detect suspicious patterns, and provide actionable intelligence for investigators.
summary: Innovation (5/5): draws on ai, artificial intelligence, ml applied to a blockchain & cybersecurity problem, placing it in the breakthrough band. Feasibility (3/5): as a software build with moderate integration complexity, a full build is tight for 36 hours and will need scope-cutting. Impact (2/5): addresses a more targeted user group within Blockchain & Cybersecurity. Tech Depth (2/5): centers on moderate engineering scope. Sustainability (3/5): will need a maintenance/upkeep plan post-hackathon. Scalability (2/5): currently scoped narrowly and would need rework to scale. Total 17/30 -> Yellow verdict.

overview.in_plain_terms: Build a tool that reads through scattered police records, call logs, and financial data, automatically pulls out people, places, and connections, and draws them as a network graph, so an investigator can see at a glance who's really connected to whom in a criminal case, instead of piecing it together by hand.
overview.why_it_matters: Investigators already have huge amounts of relevant data (FIRs, call records, financial transactions), but it's scattered across systems and formats, so critical hidden connections between suspects get missed simply because no one has time to cross-reference everything manually.
pain_points: Relevant investigative data is fragmented and unstructured across multiple systems (FIRs, CDRs, financial records, social media intelligence).
Manual cross-referencing to find hidden relationships between suspects, locations, and events is slow, labor-intensive, and error-prone.

Even when connections exist in the data, identifying which individuals are actually influential or central within a network takes specialized analytical skill most investigators don't have time to apply case by case.
overview.background: Modern criminal activities are increasingly organized and interconnected, with criminals operating through networks of associates, financial channels, and communication links. Law enforcement collects large volumes of data from FIRs, CDRs, financial records, surveillance reports, and intelligence databases, but this data is fragmented and unstructured, making manual analysis slow and prone to missing critical connections. Advances in AI, NLP, and Graph Analytics now make automated relationship discovery feasible.
overview.whats_being_asked: An AI-powered system that analyzes large volumes of structured and unstructured criminal/intelligence data to extract entities (people, locations, vehicles, phone numbers, organizations), build relationship maps, identify key influential individuals within networks, detect suspicious patterns, and provide visual and analytical insights to investigators.
expected_solution: Collection and processing of data from multiple sources.
Entity extraction: people, locations, vehicles, phone numbers, organizations.
Identification of key influential individuals within criminal networks.
Detection of suspicious patterns and unusual activities.
Visual and analytical insights delivered to investigators.

analysis.innovation_scope_note: Breakthrough band, driven by combining NLP entity extraction with graph analytics to surface hidden relationships, a genuinely powerful combination when it works, though the individual techniques (NER, graph centrality analysis) are each well-established.
analysis.invention_effort_note: Low, and this score is honest about a real constraint: without access to real, sensitive law-enforcement data (which is appropriately restricted), a hackathon team is necessarily working with a synthetic or public-proxy dataset, capping how deep the 'invention' can meaningfully go in 36 hours.

competitive_landscape.note: Entity-relationship/network-graph visualization tools are a recognizable pattern across many domains (not just crime), teams have likely seen or built similar graph-visualization demos before, differentiation comes from the entity-extraction quality and the 'key influencer' analytical layer, not the graph visualization itself.

innovation.note: NLP-driven entity extraction combined with graph-centrality analysis to surface hidden criminal-network relationships is a strong, well-matched technique-to-problem fit.

invention.note: The core techniques (NER, graph analytics) are well-established and have strong open-source library support, real hackathon effort goes into data pipeline and UI, not novel algorithms.

technical_feasibility.note: With a synthetic or public-proxy dataset and existing NLP/graph libraries (spaCy, NetworkX, Neo4j), a working demo is realistic in 36 hours.

impact_and_benefits.note: Directly useful for investigators working specific cases, a real but specialized user base rather than broad public impact.

architecture.note: Entity extraction -> graph construction -> centrality analysis -> visualization is a clean, well-understood pipeline with strong existing tooling at every stage.

overall_verdict.reasoning: A solid, technically achievable pick, especially for a team comfortable with NLP and graph libraries, the real work is building a convincing synthetic dataset that demonstrates genuinely non-obvious hidden connections, a graph that only shows relationships already explicit in the raw text won't showcase the tool's actual value.

evaluator_lens.biggest_strength: Excellent open-source tooling exists at every stage of this pipeline (spaCy for NER, NetworkX/Neo4j for graph analytics, D3.js/vis.js for visualization), making a working, visually compelling demo genuinely achievable.
evaluator_lens.biggest_risk: Without real investigative data, a synthetic dataset that's too obvious (connections already stated explicitly in the text) won't demonstrate the tool's actual analytical value, invest real thought into designing a dataset with genuinely hidden, multi-hop connections.
evaluator_lens.validate_before_commit: Confirm hour 0: design your synthetic dataset deliberately so that at least one key relationship is only discoverable by combining multiple documents/sources, not stated explicitly in any single one, that's what will make the demo actually compelling.

idea_0_4: Design a synthetic dataset of mock 'case documents' (FIRs, call logs, financial records) with deliberately embedded, non-obvious multi-hop relationships between entities.
Choose your NLP/graph stack (spaCy for entity extraction, NetworkX for graph construction/centrality analysis, a JS graph-visualization library for the frontend).
Assign owners: one on entity extraction/NLP, one on graph construction and centrality analysis, one on the visualization/investigator UI.
prototype_4_22: Build entity extraction (people, locations, phone numbers, organizations) from your synthetic text documents using NER.
Build the graph construction layer, linking extracted entities based on co-occurrence and relationship context.
Build centrality/influence analysis (e.g. betweenness or degree centrality) to identify key individuals within the constructed network.
integration_22_30: Wire the full pipeline: documents in -> entities extracted -> graph built -> key-individual analysis -> visual output.
Test specifically whether your tool surfaces the deliberately-hidden multi-hop connection you designed into your dataset, this is your core proof of value.
Add suspicious-pattern detection (e.g. flagging unusual transaction timing or repeated location co-occurrence) as a secondary analytical layer.
polish_30_36: Build a clean, interactive graph visualization for the investigator-facing demo, this is inherently visual and should be the centerpiece.
Prepare a clear narrative: walk through your synthetic case, show the hidden connection the tool surfaced that wouldn't be obvious from any single document.
Be honest about the synthetic nature of your data and what real deployment would require (access to real, appropriately authorized case data).
build_plan.how_to_stand_out: Structure the demo as a mystery: show judges 3-4 raw 'case documents' first and ask if they can spot the hidden connection, then run your tool and show it surfacing that same connection automatically. That framing makes the tool's value viscerally obvious rather than just described.

strengths: Strong, mature open-source tooling across the entire pipeline makes this a genuinely achievable, low-technical-risk build.
Graph visualization is inherently compelling and easy for any judge to understand and evaluate.
weaknesses: No access to real investigative data means all demonstrated value depends on the quality and cleverness of a synthetic dataset design.
Real-world unstructured data (informal language, inconsistent naming, OCR errors from scanned records) is much messier than clean synthetic text, a caveat worth acknowledging honestly.

team_fit.ideal_ratio: 1 NLP, 1 graph/backend, 1 frontend, roughly even, each piece is genuinely necessary and none should be shortchanged.
team_fit.approach: Design the synthetic dataset collaboratively as a team exercise first, since its quality (specifically, how well it embeds non-obvious connections) determines how compelling the entire demo will be, this is worth real deliberate time investment.

ai_buildability_split.ai_can_build_fast: NER pipeline setup, graph-construction code, and centrality-analysis implementation using existing libraries can all be built quickly with AI coding assistance.
ai_buildability_split.needs_human_judgment: Designing a synthetic dataset with genuinely realistic, non-obvious multi-hop relationships needs real human creativity and case-study thinking, this isn't something to auto-generate carelessly, a weak dataset undermines the whole demo.
ai_buildability_split.risk_of_leaning_on_ai_only: An AI-generated synthetic dataset where all relationships are stated explicitly and obviously in the text will make the entity-extraction and graph tools look impressive but won't actually demonstrate the tool's real analytical value, invest real design effort here.

data_resource_availability.status: No real law-enforcement investigative data is publicly available or appropriate for this use case; public academic criminal-network-analysis research and datasets (from published criminology papers) can inform realistic synthetic data design.
data_resource_availability.backup_plan: If team creativity for synthetic case design runs thin, base the network structure loosely on publicly documented (and already prosecuted/public-record) organized crime case studies, adapted and fictionalized, rather than inventing patterns with no grounding.

judge_qna.question: How would this perform on real, messy investigative data versus your clean synthetic dataset?
judge_qna.strong_answer: We're upfront that real unstructured data (informal language, OCR errors, inconsistent naming across sources) is messier than our synthetic test set, our NLP pipeline would need additional robustness work, entity resolution and disambiguation especially, for real deployment.
judge_qna.follow_up: What specific entity-resolution challenge do you think would be hardest with real data?

judge_qna.question: How do you identify 'key influential individuals', what's the actual metric?
judge_qna.strong_answer: We used [specific graph-centrality metric, e.g. betweenness centrality to find bridge individuals connecting otherwise separate clusters], here's why that metric makes sense for identifying influence in a criminal network specifically.
judge_qna.follow_up: What would a different centrality metric (e.g. degree vs betweenness) tell you differently about network structure?

judge_qna.question: What are the privacy and due-process implications of a tool like this?
judge_qna.strong_answer: This is intended as an investigative aid to surface leads for further human investigation, not as evidence or grounds for action on its own, real deployment would need clear policy on how outputs are used and reviewed by trained investigators.
judge_qna.follow_up: How would you prevent this tool's output from being over-relied upon as if it were confirmed fact?
